title: Matrix coefficients of a finite-dimensional comodule form a subcoalgebra
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $C$ be a $k$-vector space with linear maps $\Delta:C\to C\otimes_k C$ and $\epsilon:C\to k$ satisfying coassociativity and both counit identities; tensor products use [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. A right $C$-comodule is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a linear map $\rho:M\to M\otimes_k C$ satisfying $(\rho\otimes1_C)\rho=(1_M\otimes\Delta)\rho$ and $(1_M\otimes\epsilon)\rho=1_M$, under the canonical associativity and unit identifications. Assume $M$ is finite-dimensional [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace], and let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be any basis indexed by a finite set $I$. Define $c_{ij}\in C$ by $\rho(e_j)=\sum_{i\in I}e_i\otimes c_{ij}$, and put $D=\operatorname{span}_k\{c_{ij}:i,j\in I\}\subset C$. Then $\Delta(c_{ij})=\sum_{a\in I}c_{ia}\otimes c_{aj}$ and $\epsilon(c_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$. The space $D$ is finite-dimensional, and the restrictions of $\Delta$ and $\epsilon$ give it a counital coassociative coalgebra structure for which its inclusion in $C$ is a coalgebra homomorphism. Here $D\otimes_kD$ is identified with its image in $C\otimes_kC$. The case $I=\varnothing$ is included.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175, displayed matrix-coefficient identities and the paragraph defining the subcoalgebra C_V immediately before Theorem 9.32.

proof.text: Let $e_i^*:M\to k$ be the coordinate functional of the given basis, so $e_i^*(e_a)=\delta_{ia}$. By [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], the bilinear map $(m,x)\mapsto e_i^*(m)x$ induces $T_i:M\otimes_k C\to C$. Expanding $m=\sum_i e_i^*(m)e_i$ in each pure tensor, then using that pure tensors span, gives $t=\sum_i e_i\otimes T_i(t)$ for every $t\in M\otimes_k C$. Applying $T_i$ also proves uniqueness of these coefficients. Thus $c_{ij}=T_i(\rho(e_j))$ are well-defined, including when the basis is empty.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175, displayed matrix-coefficient identities and the paragraph defining the subcoalgebra C_V immediately before Theorem 9.32.

proof.text: Evaluate comodule coassociativity at $e_j$. Under the stated associativity identification its two sides are $\sum_{b,a}e_b\otimes c_{ba}\otimes c_{aj}$ and $\sum_a e_a\otimes\Delta(c_{aj})$. Apply the linear map induced by $(m,x,y)\mapsto e_i^*(m)(x\otimes y)$, whose existence follows by two applications of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The resulting equality is $\sum_a c_{ia}\otimes c_{aj}=\Delta(c_{ij})$. This uses no independence assumption on the $c_{ij}$.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175, displayed matrix-coefficient identities and the paragraph defining the subcoalgebra C_V immediately before Theorem 9.32.

proof.text: Evaluate the comodule counit identity at $e_j$. It gives $\sum_a\epsilon(c_{aj})e_a=e_j$. Applying the coordinate functional $e_i^*$ yields $\epsilon(c_{ij})=\delta_{ij}$. The scalar-valued tensor map used here is induced by the bilinear map $(m,x)\mapsto\epsilon(x)m$ in [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product].

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175, displayed matrix-coefficient identities and the paragraph defining the subcoalgebra C_V immediately before Theorem 9.32.

proof.text: The family $(c_{ij})$ is finite because $I\times I$ is finite. Its span $D$ consists of its linear combinations, so these finitely many elements span $D$; this is exactly finite-dimensionality in [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. If $I=\varnothing$, the span of the empty family is $D=0$.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175, displayed matrix-coefficient identities and the paragraph defining the subcoalgebra C_V immediately before Theorem 9.32.

proof.text: Write $\iota:D\hookrightarrow C$. Apply [lem-trf-vector-subspace-complement] over the field $k$ to choose $C=D\oplus Q$. The projection $p:C\to D$, defined by $p(d+q)=d$, is linear by uniqueness of the decomposition, and $p\iota=1_D$. The maps induced on tensors by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] satisfy $(p\otimes p)(\iota\otimes\iota)=1$ and $p^{\otimes3}\iota^{\otimes3}=1$: on pure tensors these are just $p(\iota(d))=d$, and pure tensors span. Hence $\iota^{\otimes2}$ and $\iota^{\otimes3}$ are injective. This justifies the required image identification without assuming that tensoring arbitrary module inclusions is injective.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175, displayed matrix-coefficient identities and the paragraph defining the subcoalgebra C_V immediately before Theorem 9.32.

proof.text: Define linear maps $\Delta_D=(p\otimes p)\Delta\iota:D\to D\otimes_kD$ and $\epsilon_D=\epsilon\iota:D\to k$, using [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The identity from step 2 gives $\Delta_D(c_{ij})=\sum_a c_{ia}\otimes_k c_{aj}$, since $p$ fixes each coefficient. Therefore $(\iota\otimes\iota)\Delta_D=\Delta\iota$ on the spanning coefficients and hence on $D$. Injectivity from step 5 shows that $\Delta_D$ is precisely the restriction of $\Delta$ to $D$, uniquely determined and independent of $Q$.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175, displayed matrix-coefficient identities and the paragraph defining the subcoalgebra C_V immediately before Theorem 9.32.

proof.text: To check coassociativity on $D$, apply the injective map $\iota^{\otimes3}$ to its two proposed sides. By step 6 and functoriality of tensor maps in [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], these become $(\Delta\otimes1_C)\Delta\iota$ and $(1_C\otimes\Delta)\Delta\iota$, which agree by coassociativity on $C$. For either counit law, apply $\iota$; the images become respectively $(\epsilon\otimes1_C)\Delta\iota$ and $(1_C\otimes\epsilon)\Delta\iota$, both equal to $\iota$ by the two counit laws on $C$. Cancel the injective maps. Thus $D$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra; step 6 and $\epsilon_D=\epsilon\iota$ say exactly that $\iota$ is a coalgebra homomorphism. For $D=0$ all these equations hold between zero maps, so the empty case is included.

source.place: §9(d), printed pp.174–175, displayed matrix-coefficient identities and the paragraph defining the subcoalgebra C_V immediately before Theorem 9.32.
